paragraphs.heading: What a virus is
paragraphs.text: A virus is an infectious agent too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, and it can make copies of itself only inside living cells. Viruses infect every kind of life, from animals and plants to bacteria and archaea. They turn up in nearly every ecosystem and are the most numerous type of biological entity. Their study is called virology, a branch of microbiology.

paragraphs.heading: The virus particle
paragraphs.text: Outside a cell, a virus exists as a separate particle called a virion. It is made of genetic material, long molecules of DNA or RNA; a protein coat called the capsid that protects it; and in some cases an outer envelope of lipids. Shapes range from simple helices and icosahedrons to more complex forms. Most are about a hundredth the size of most bacteria. Once a virus gets into a host cell, the cell is often forced to make thousands of copies of it quickly.

paragraphs.heading: Alive or not
paragraphs.text: Some biologists treat viruses as living, because they hold genetic material, multiply, and evolve by natural selection. But they lack features usually seen as necessary for life, such as a cell structure. Because they have some of these qualities but not all, viruses have been called organisms at the edge of life.

paragraphs.heading: How viruses spread
paragraphs.text: Viruses travel in several ways. Some ride in vectors, organisms that carry disease: aphids feeding on sap move viruses from plant to plant, and blood-sucking insects can carry viruses of animals. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, chickenpox, smallpox and measles spread through the air in coughs and sneezes. Norovirus and rotavirus pass by the faecal–oral route, through hands, food or water, and fewer than 100 norovirus particles can infect a person. HIV spreads through sexual contact and infected blood.

paragraphs.heading: Fighting back
paragraphs.text: The range of host cells a virus can infect is its host range, which may be narrow or broad. In animals, infection sets off an immune response that usually clears the virus. Vaccines can produce such a response artificially, giving immunity to one specific viral infection. Some viruses, such as those behind HIV/AIDS, HPV infection and viral hepatitis, escape the immune response and cause chronic infections. Around 100 antiviral drugs or drug combinations are used worldwide.

paragraphs.heading: Where viruses came from
paragraphs.text: How viruses began is still unclear, and because they leave no fossils, scientists use molecular methods to look back. One idea is that viruses were once small cells living as parasites in larger cells, which lost the genes their way of life did not need. The bacteria rickettsia and chlamydia, which also reproduce only inside host cells, support this idea. Another is that some viruses began as bits of DNA or RNA that escaped from a larger organism's genes, such as plasmids or transposons, once called jumping genes.

paragraphs.heading: The name and the first virus
paragraphs.text: The word virus comes from Latin for poison and other harmful liquids. It came to mean an agent of infectious disease in 1728, long before Martinus Beijerinck and Dmitri Ivanovsky discovered viruses in the late 19th century. The first virus found was the tobacco mosaic virus, in the 1890s. There are millions of virus species, and more than 16,000 have since been described in detail.
